prose.text: "Can users still sign in to a personal or third-party tenant of this SaaS app?" is answered by a tenant profile and the Cloud App Control (CAC) rule that uses it. {{what-it-is}} Despite the name, this is not a multi-tenancy feature. {{not-microtenants}}

prose.label: What a profile is.
prose.text: {{one-app-per-profile}} {{create-form}} The profile does nothing until a CAC rule references it: {{rule-reference-field}} How a rule's criteria combine is in [[zia.cloud-app-control.rule-criteria:criteria-expression]], rule order in [[zia.cloud-app-control.precedence:cac-rule-order]], and the per-category rule cap in [[zia.cloud-app-control.rule-types:rule-cap-per-category]].

items.text: Why the restriction works at all, and which headers ZIA adds: [[zia.tenant-profiles.wire-mechanic]].
The SSL/TLS inspection rules the restriction needs, per application: [[zia.tenant-profiles.ssl-prerequisite]].

Which applications are supported and what each profile holds: [[zia.tenant-profiles.applications]], with per-application options in [[zia.tenant-profiles.app-specifics]] and Microsoft's two versions in [[zia.tenant-profiles.microsoft]].
Caps per rule, profile and organization: [[zia.tenant-profiles.limits]].
API, SDK and Terraform behavior, including the older provider cap: [[zia.tenant-profiles.api-surface]].
The AI & ML rule flow, where Tenant Profiles appears for ChatGPT: [[zia.cloud-app-control.ai-ml-rules:tenant-profiles-visibility]].

prose.label: Open points.
prose.text: What deleting a profile that a rule uses does is open {{gap:delete-referenced-profile}}. What a stale identifier does after a tenant change is open {{gap:identity-change-staleness}}.

what-it-is.statement: Tenancy restriction lets you restrict access to personal accounts, business accounts, or both for certain cloud applications. It has two parts: creating tenant profiles, and associating them with Cloud App Control policy rules.

quotes: Zscaler's tenancy restriction feature allows you to restrict access either to personal accounts, business accounts, or both for certain cloud applications.
It consists of two parts: creating tenant profiles and associating them with the Cloud App Control policy rules.

one-app-per-profile.statement: Each tenant profile is created for one cloud application; the Tenant Profiles page lists a Cloud Application and its configuration details for every profile.

quotes: Cloud Application: The cloud application for which the tenant profile is created (e.g., Dropbox, Google, Microsoft Login Services).
For each tenant profile, you can see the following:
Details: The configuration details of the tenant profile.

not-microtenants.statement: A tenant profile is a SaaS-application tenant object. It is not a ZIA sub-tenant, microtenant or MSP-scoping setting.
not-microtenants.conditions: No source contrasts tenant profiles with microtenants. This follows from the definition: the profile names a cloud application and identifiers inside it.

create-form.statement: A tenant profile needs a unique name, which is the label shown when configuring Cloud App Control rules. The description is optional and cannot exceed 10,240 characters.

quotes: In the Tenant Profile Name field, enter a unique name for the tenant profile.
This name is displayed while configuring the respective Cloud App Control policy rules.
Description: (Optional) Enter any additional comments or information.

rule-reference-field.statement: A Cloud App Control rule holds its tenant profiles in `tenancyProfileIds` (Terraform `tenancy_profile_ids`), a list of profile references.

allow-blocks-others.statement: Allowing a specific tenant automatically blocks other tenants for most cloud applications, and subsequent policies are not evaluated.

quotes: Allowing a specific tenant automatically blocks other tenants for most of the cloud applications, and subsequent policies are not evaluated.

youtube-aws-explicit-block.statement: For YouTube and Amazon Web Services, subsequent policies are still evaluated after the allow, so an explicit block policy is required to block other tenants.

quotes: However, for YouTube and Amazon Web Services, subsequent policies are evaluated, so an explicit block policy is required to block other tenants for them.
Allowing a specific tenant automatically blocks other tenants for most of the cloud applications, and subsequent policies are not evaluated.

delete-referenced-profile.title: What happens when a tenant profile in use by a rule is deleted
delete-referenced-profile.detail: Unverified legacy statement: "If a tenant profile is deleted, CAC rules referencing it may behave unexpectedly - the profile reference becomes stale. ZIA does not prevent deletion of profiles referenced by active rules." No captured source states whether the delete is refused, cascades, or leaves a dangling reference. The Help article says only that the profile version cannot be changed while the profile is associated with a policy (Microsoft). Resolve by deleting a referenced profile in a scratch tenant and re-reading the rule.
delete-referenced-profile.blocks: advising whether a profile can be deleted before detaching it from rules

identity-change-staleness.title: What a stale tenant identifier does after a tenant migration or domain rename
identity-change-staleness.detail: Unverified legacy statement: "If the Azure AD directory ID or Google Workspace primary domain changes (tenant migration, merger, domain rename), the Tenant Profile's item_data_primary becomes stale. The profile keeps matching at the rule level, but ... the SaaS vendor rejects or misidentifies the tenant. No Zscaler-side error is visible." No source describes validation of identifiers or what the vendor does with a wrong one, apart from Slack (see the app-specifics subject). Resolve with a lab test using a deliberately wrong identifier.
identity-change-staleness.blocks: knowing whether a wrong identifier fails closed or open
